projects.title: Helix
projects.subtitle: Self-Hosted Localhost Tunneling Tool
projects.description: An ngrok alternative that exposes localhost on persistent, path-based public URLs instead of disposable subdomains. CLI-first, self-hosted relay, passwordless email-code auth.

caseStudy.challenge: Existing tunneling tools like ngrok hand out disposable subdomains on every restart, offer no self-hosting story, and charge for basics like persistent URLs. Developers demoing work-in-progress need a stable, shareable link without standing up their own infrastructure from scratch — but they also don't want to hand traffic to a third party they don't control.
caseStudy.solution: Built Helix around path-based routing instead of subdomains — every tunnel lives at a persistent /tunnel/{name}/ path, claimed once and reused. The relay is self-hostable, so traffic stays on infrastructure the user controls. Auth is passwordless (email one-time code), shared across web and CLI. Handled the hard part of path-based routing: rewriting relative asset URLs in tunneled responses so they resolve under the path prefix instead of breaking against the relay's root.
impact: Delivered a working ngrok alternative with zero ongoing hosting cost via Render's free tier
Solved the relative-URL breakage problem inherent to path-based (non-subdomain) tunneling
Shipped passwordless auth shared cleanly across CLI and web dashboard
Built a Pro tier (unlimited tunnels, 24h idle timeout, password-locked tunnels, request history) as a real monetization path
Took the product from idea to full build in 4-5 days
features: Path-based persistent tunnels (/tunnel/{name}/) instead of disposable subdomains
Self-hosted relay — traffic stays on infrastructure you control
Passwordless email-code authentication, shared across CLI and web
Live request history dashboard
Password-protected tunnels (Pro)
Simple two-command flow: helix login, helix myapp 3000
techStack: Node.js relay server + CLI client, TypeScript throughout
Render (free tier) for hosting, with uptime pinging to prevent idle spin-down
lessons: Path-based routing is viable but requires rewriting relative asset URLs server-side — a subdomain-based tool doesn't have this problem
Free-tier hosting is workable for a real product if you actively manage idle spin-down
GitHub OAuth costs more build time than a plain API token but fits a developer-tool audience better
Shipping a full product (not just an MVP) in 4-5 days is possible with tight scope discipline

projects.title: Radon
projects.subtitle: Provider-Agnostic Backend SDK Suite
projects.description: One typed API across auth, payments, storage, email, and AI — 126+ providers, swappable by config instead of code, self-hosted with zero lock-in.

caseStudy.challenge: Every product ends up gluing together five separate vendor SDKs for auth, payments, storage, email, and AI — each with its own auth scheme, quirks, and webhook shape. Switching providers later (Stripe to Paystack, S3 to R2) usually means a rewrite, not a config change. Most existing solutions solve this by becoming a hosted service with per-user pricing and full data lock-in.
caseStudy.solution: Built Radon as five SDKs sharing one interface shape: auth, payments, storage, email, and AI, each normalizing 10-50+ providers behind a single typed call (auth(), charge(), upload(), send(), chat()). Provider-specific quirks are absorbed inside each adapter and never leak into calling code. Everything runs against the developer's own infrastructure and provider keys — no hosted service, no stored secrets, no per-MAU pricing. Escape hatches (native()/rawClient()) cover the 20% of cases the unified API doesn't.
impact: Shipped 126+ provider integrations across 5 SDKs with zero runtime dependencies
Free tier is genuinely production-grade (not a crippled trial) — full MIT-licensed core across all 5 SDKs
Pro tier priced as a single $7.99 lifetime license unlocking every SDK, unlimited projects — no subscription
Built adapters lazy-load, so an app using only OpenAI + Anthropic never bundles the other providers
Designed the suite to expand (payments, storage, AI added after auth validated the model)
features: One typed interface per domain (auth, payments, storage, email, AI) across 10-50 providers each
Provider swap by config change, never a code rewrite
Self-hosted — no account, no hosted service, runs against your own DB and provider keys
Escape hatches to the native provider client for edge cases
Zero required runtime dependencies, ESM + CJS, strict TypeScript
Single lifetime license unlocks Pro across the entire suite
techStack: TypeScript, Node.js ≥18, ESM + CJS dual build
Framework-agnostic (Next.js, Express, Fastify, Hono, NestJS, and more)
Database-agnostic auth adapters (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB, Firebase, and more)
Normalized webhook handling across payment/email providers
lessons: Generalizing auth logic already built twice (in two prior projects) into a real SDK surfaced most of the hard edge cases early
A lifetime one-off price removes the friction of a subscription decision for indie developers
Keeping the free tier fully complete (not a trial) is a stronger trust signal than a generous trial period
Scoping v1 to JS/TS only, deferring other languages, kept the "zero hosting, zero liability" pitch intact

projects.title: Kroma
projects.subtitle: MCP Server for AI Design Intelligence
projects.description: A Model Context Protocol server that gives AI coding agents live access to the design web — real UI inspiration, component code, and motion techniques — so agents stop shipping generic layouts.

caseStudy.challenge: AI coding agents design from memory, which converges on the same visual defaults — centered divs, gray gradients, the same handful of fonts. There was no way for an agent to look up current, real design work the way a human designer browses Dribbble or Awwwards before building.
caseStudy.solution: Built Kroma as a stateless MCP server exposing six tools that let any MCP-compatible agent search live design sources in real time: UI inspiration from galleries like Mobbin and Awwwards, copy-pasteable component code from shadcn/Magic UI/Aceternity, motion and shader techniques from CodePen/Shadertoy/GSAP sources, a site design scraper, an open-ended design-web search, and a source registry lookup. Resolves results through the Serper API so agents get live data instead of hallucinated recommendations.
impact: Published as an open-source npm package (@kromamcp/server), installable with a single npx command, no local setup
Compatible with every major MCP host: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex CLI, Roo Code, Cline, Zed, VS Code
Five of six tools work on Serper's free tier — only image-based inspiration search needs a paid plan
Curated source registry spans 31 sources across inspiration, components, and effects
features: kroma_find_ui_inspiration — mood-boards from live design galleries
kroma_find_component_code — real, copy-pasteable component code from doc sites
kroma_find_effects_and_shaders — GLSL/canvas/GSAP/Framer Motion techniques
kroma_scrape_site_design — reverse-engineers a site's type, palette, and stack
kroma_search_design_web — open-ended fallback search
kroma_list_sources — offline source registry lookup, no API key required
techStack: Serper API for live search resolution
Runs over stdio for any MCP-compatible host
lessons: Giving an agent search tools scoped to a specific problem (design references) works better than a generic web search tool
Keeping the tool stateless and API-key-optional (for the offline source list) lowers the adoption barrier significantly
MIT-licensing an infrastructure-adjacent tool like this builds credibility faster than a closed beta would

projects.title: Savice
projects.subtitle: Premium Tennis Court Booking Platform
projects.description: A booking and coaching platform for tennis players — court reservations, professional coach matching, and performance tracking, built with a bold dark-navy and lime design system.

caseStudy.challenge: Tennis facilities typically split court booking, coach discovery, and performance tracking across disconnected tools (or no tools at all). Serious players want one platform that handles booking, training, and progress in a single, well-designed experience rather than a generic sports-club website template.
caseStudy.solution: Designed Savice around three pillars — court booking, professional coaching, and performance tracking — unified under a bold dark-navy (#0A0F1E) and lime-green (#CBFF4D) design system that reads as premium and athletic rather than generic. Built the full component system from scratch: a scroll-aware navbar with backdrop blur, an animated hero with full-width SVG background, coach profile cards, tiered programme pricing, and an FAQ accordion — all on Next.js 16 with Framer Motion throughout.
impact: Built a complete, production-styled marketing site with booking, coaching, and programme-pricing flows
Established a distinctive dark/lime visual identity that stands apart from typical sports-booking templates
Structured programme tiers (Beginner/Intermediate/Advanced) with clear pricing and duration
Built reusable components (navbar, hero, FAQ, footer) intended to extend into the full booking product
features: Court booking flow with real-time availability framing
Coach profiles with specialty tagging (serve/technique, strategy/mental, fitness/agility)
Tiered training programmes with per-month pricing
Scroll-triggered navbar backdrop blur and full-width animated hero
FAQ accordion and testimonial sections
Responsive layout across booking, about, pricing, docs, and contact pages
lessons: A distinctive color system (dark navy + lime) does more to differentiate a booking platform than any single feature
Scroll-aware nav interactions are a small detail that meaningfully raises perceived polish
Structuring programme tiers clearly upfront makes pricing pages easier to build than retrofitting them later

projects.title: Solaris
projects.subtitle: Residential & Commercial Solar Marketing Site
projects.description: A conversion-focused marketing site for a solar installation company — eligibility checks, instant quotes, and a 3-week install pitch, framed around real savings numbers.

caseStudy.challenge: Solar companies compete on trust and clarity as much as price — prospective customers are wary of hidden fees, slow installs, and vague savings claims. The site needed to make the value proposition (up to 80% bill reduction, fast install) immediately legible while feeling premium enough to justify a considered purchase decision.
caseStudy.solution: Built Solaris as a single-page, conversion-first marketing site structured around a simple three-step funnel: check eligibility, get a free quote, get installed. Led with hard numbers (500+ homes powered, $2M+ saved, 4.9★ rating) directly in the hero to establish credibility fast, backed by specific customer testimonials with real before/after bill figures.
impact: Structured the entire page around a clear 3-step conversion funnel (eligibility → quote → install)
Used concrete social-proof numbers (homes powered, dollars saved, rating) instead of generic marketing copy
Built testimonial section with specific, believable savings figures rather than vague praise
Delivered a clean, fast-loading marketing site optimized for a single conversion action (Get Free Quote)
features: Three-step 'How it works' flow: eligibility check, free quote, professional install
Hero-level trust stats (homes powered, years of experience, satisfaction rating, dollars saved)
Customer testimonials with specific bill-reduction figures
Repeated, prominent CTA placement ('Get Free Quote') throughout the scroll
lessons: Leading with specific numbers (not just claims) builds trust faster on a single-page conversion site
A tight three-step funnel outperforms a feature-heavy page for service businesses selling a considered purchase
Testimonials with concrete before/after figures read as more credible than generic praise quotes
